subject: history_geography
name: History, Geography & Civics

pillars.name: Historical & Geographic Thinking
pillars.scope: The student holds a wrong idea about how the past or places work: causes, change, significance, perspective, people-environment links.

pillars.name: Argument & Inquiry
pillars.scope: The thinking may be sound, but the argument or inquiry is set up wrongly: off the question, no arguable thesis, no criteria, one-sided, badly ordered.

pillars.name: Evidence & Sources
pillars.scope: The argument is sound, but proving it goes wrong: narrating instead of analysing, no or unexplained evidence, sources taken at face value, data misread.

pillars.name: Facts & Recall
pillars.scope: The reasoning is sound; a date, name, term, place, statistic or calculation slips.

pillars.name: Communication
pillars.scope: The ideas are sound, but the expression gets in the way: unclear, informal, imprecise terms, missing citations or map conventions.

pillars.name: Test Habits
pillars.scope: How the student handles the task: blanks, unfinished or missed parts, length, ignoring the provided source.

decision_order: Does the student hold a wrong idea about cause, change, significance, perspective or people-environment links (CON)?
Is the thinking right but the argument or inquiry set up wrongly (STR)?
Is the argument right but the evidence or source work weak (PRC)?
Is it a slip in a date, name, term, place, number or calculation (FAC)?
Are the ideas right but expressed unclearly, informally or without citation or map conventions (COM)?
Or is it how the task was handled (TST)?

codes.name: Presentism
codes.plain_name: Judged the past only by today's values
codes.student_help: Ask what people at the time believed and why, before you judge them.
codes.description: Judges past people or events only by present-day values, without considering the beliefs and conditions of the time.
codes.example: 'People in 1917 were stupid for supporting conscription.'

tell_apart.how: If the student treats a past group as all thinking the same, use CON_UNIFORM_GROUPS.
If the student considers only one side of a question, use STR_ONE_SIDED.

codes.name: Single Cause
codes.plain_name: Gave only one cause for a complex event
codes.student_help: Big events usually have several causes: long-term and short-term, political, economic and social.
codes.description: Explains a complex event with one cause, or confuses a trigger with the underlying causes.
codes.example: 'World War I happened because Franz Ferdinand was shot.'

tell_apart.how: If the issue is judging importance rather than cause, use CON_SIGNIFICANCE_AS_FAME.

codes.name: Change Always Progress
codes.plain_name: Assumed change is always progress
codes.student_help: Change can be better for some and worse for others; some things stay the same.
codes.description: Assumes all change is improvement for everyone, or misses continuity alongside change.
codes.example: 'After 1918 women had full equality in Canada because some women could vote.'

tell_apart.how: If the error is treating a group as uniform, use CON_UNIFORM_GROUPS.

codes.remediation: Tier 1: continuity-and-change timeline with winners and losers.

codes.name: Significance as Fame
codes.plain_name: Judged importance by fame or size
codes.student_help: Something is significant if it had deep, lasting effects on many people, or reveals something important.
codes.description: Judges historical or geographic significance by how famous, dramatic or large something is, not by its consequences or what it reveals.
codes.example: 'The Halifax Explosion is the most significant event because it was the biggest explosion.'

tell_apart.how: If the student gives no criteria at all, use STR_NO_CRITERIA; this code is about using the wrong idea of significance.

codes.remediation: Tier 1: significance criteria (impact, depth, duration, revealing).

codes.name: Groups Treated as Uniform
codes.plain_name: Treated a whole group as all the same
codes.student_help: People in a group (Canadians, a province, a community) often disagreed; name who thought what.
codes.description: Treats a nation, group or community as if everyone in it shared the same experience or view.
codes.example: 'Canadians all supported the war effort.'

tell_apart.how: If the issue is judging the past by today's values, use CON_PRESENTISM.

codes.remediation: Tier 1: perspectives grid with several groups.

codes.name: Environment Decides Everything
codes.plain_name: Assumed geography alone decides what people do
codes.student_help: Physical geography shapes choices, but people, technology, economics and policy matter too.
codes.description: Explains human patterns (settlement, wealth, culture) by physical geography alone, or treats natural and human systems as unconnected.
codes.example: 'Northern Canada has few people only because it is cold.'

tell_apart.how: CON_SINGLE_CAUSE is the general one-cause error; use this code when that cause is physical geography.

codes.name: Off the Prompt
codes.plain_name: Wrote about something other than the prompt
codes.student_help: Turn the prompt into a question and make sure your thesis answers it.
codes.description: The response or thesis addresses a different question or topic from the one set (writes about a character when asked about a theme, or a general opinion when asked about the text).
codes.example: Asked how the Depression changed government's role, writes about the causes of the stock market crash.

tell_apart.how: If one part of the question is left out, use TST_SKIPPED_PART.

codes.name: No Arguable Thesis
codes.plain_name: Thesis isn't something you can argue
codes.student_help: A thesis is a claim someone could disagree with, plus why.
codes.description: The thesis is a fact, a plot statement, an announcement ('In this essay I will...'), or is missing.
codes.example: 'The Winnipeg General Strike happened in 1919.'

tell_apart.how: If the thesis is arguable but answers another question, use STR_OFF_PROMPT.

codes.remediation: Tier 2: claim + because + so-what thesis frame.

codes.name: No Criteria
codes.plain_name: Judged without saying how
codes.student_help: When you judge (most significant, biggest change), say what you are judging by.
codes.description: Makes a judgement of significance, change, success or responsibility without stating or applying criteria.
codes.example: 'Vimy Ridge was the most important battle.' with no reason for 'important'.

tell_apart.how: If criteria are used but they are about fame or size, use CON_SIGNIFICANCE_AS_FAME.

codes.name: One-Sided
codes.plain_name: Looked at only one side or perspective
codes.student_help: Include the perspectives the question asks for, especially those of groups most affected.
codes.description: Considers only one perspective when the question asks for several, or leaves out the groups most affected (for example Indigenous peoples, workers, women, immigrants).
codes.example: Explains the building of the CPR only from the government's point of view.

tell_apart.how: If the student treats one group as uniform, use CON_UNIFORM_GROUPS.

codes.name: Weak Inquiry Question
codes.plain_name: Inquiry question has a yes/no or one-fact answer
codes.student_help: Good inquiry questions start with how, why, to what extent, or how significant.
codes.description: In inquiry tasks, poses a question answerable with a fact or yes/no, or too broad to investigate.
codes.example: 'When did Canada join NATO?'

tell_apart.how: STR_NO_ARGUABLE_THESIS is about the claim; this code is about the question being investigated.

codes.name: Illogical Order
codes.plain_name: Ideas aren't in a logical order
codes.student_help: Put ideas in an order that builds: time order, weakest to strongest, or cause to effect.
codes.description: Ideas or paragraphs are ordered with no logic or progression; the argument jumps back and forth.
codes.example: Jumps from 1945 to 1914 to 1982 with no thematic reason.

tell_apart.how: If the order is fine but sentences are hard to follow, use COM_UNCLEAR_SENTENCES.

codes.name: Narrative Instead of Analysis
codes.plain_name: Told what happened instead of explaining it
codes.student_help: After each event, explain how it answers the question (why, how much, how significant).
codes.description: Narrates events in order where explanation or argument is asked for.
codes.example: Asked why the Statute of Westminster mattered, lists events from 1919 to 1931.

tell_apart.how: If evidence is given with a point but not linked, use PRC_EVIDENCE_NOT_EXPLAINED.

codes.name: No Evidence
codes.plain_name: Made a claim without evidence
codes.student_help: Back each point with a quote or specific detail from the text.
codes.description: Makes claims about a text without any quotation, specific reference or detail.
codes.example: 'The Depression was very bad for farmers.' with nothing specific.

tell_apart.how: If evidence is given but not explained, use PRC_EVIDENCE_NOT_EXPLAINED.

codes.name: Evidence Not Explained
codes.plain_name: Didn't explain how the quote proves the point
codes.student_help: After a quote, explain which words matter and how they prove your point.
codes.description: Gives a relevant quotation and then moves on, or only restates it, without explaining how it supports the claim.
codes.example: 'Unemployment hit 30% in 1933.' and the paragraph ends.

tell_apart.how: If the paragraph is mostly narrative, use PRC_NARRATIVE_NOT_ANALYSIS.

codes.name: Source Taken at Face Value
codes.plain_name: Trusted a source without questioning it
codes.student_help: Ask who made the source, when, why, and for whom before you trust it.
codes.description: Uses a source without considering its author, date, purpose or bias (propaganda posters treated as fact).
codes.example: 'The poster shows that every Canadian man was eager to enlist.'

tell_apart.how: If the student uses several sources but ignores where they disagree, use PRC_SOURCES_NOT_CORROBORATED.

codes.remediation: Tier 2: sourcing questions (author, date, purpose, audience).

codes.name: Sources Not Compared
codes.plain_name: Didn't compare sources
codes.student_help: Check whether other sources agree; explain any disagreement.
codes.description: Uses sources without comparing them, ignores sources that disagree, or picks only the one that fits.
codes.example: Uses one politician's speech as proof of public opinion while ignoring the provided strike newspaper.

tell_apart.how: If one source is accepted uncritically, use PRC_SOURCE_AT_FACE_VALUE.

codes.name: Data, Map or Graph Misread
codes.plain_name: Misread a map, graph or table
codes.student_help: Read the title, legend, axes and scale before you read the data.
codes.description: Misreads a map, climate graph, population pyramid, table or chart (wrong axis, scale or legend).
codes.example: Reads the precipitation bars on a climate graph against the temperature axis.

tell_apart.how: If the error is locating a place, use FAC_PLACE_LOCATION.
If the student draws a map or graph missing its conventions, use COM_MAP_CONVENTIONS.

codes.name: Date or Chronology Slip
codes.plain_name: Got a date or order of events wrong
codes.student_help: Check dates against your timeline.
codes.description: Gives a wrong date or puts events in the wrong order.
codes.example: 'Confederation happened in 1876.'

tell_apart.how: If the chronology error supports a wrong cause-and-effect claim, also check CON_SINGLE_CAUSE.

codes.name: Name or Term Recall Slip
codes.plain_name: Used the wrong name or term
codes.student_help: Check names of people, laws and events in your notes.
codes.description: Uses the wrong name for a person, law, treaty, event or concept.
codes.example: Calls the Indian Act the 'Indigenous Act' or confuses Mackenzie King with Laurier.

tell_apart.how: If the student uses an everyday word instead of the term, use COM_IMPRECISE_TERMS.

codes.name: Place or Location Slip
codes.plain_name: Got a place or location wrong
codes.student_help: Check latitude/longitude order and the map's scale and grid.
codes.description: Locates a place wrongly, swaps latitude and longitude, or uses grid references or scale wrongly.
codes.example: Places Saskatchewan east of Manitoba; gives 45° W, 75° N for Ottawa.

tell_apart.how: If the error is reading a data map or graph, use PRC_DATA_MISREAD.

codes.name: Statistic or Fact Slip
codes.plain_name: Remembered a fact or number wrongly
codes.student_help: Check this fact or number in your notes or the source.
codes.description: Misremembers a statistic or specific fact.
codes.example: 'About 6,000 Canadians died at Vimy Ridge' (about 3,600).

tell_apart.how: If the number was in a provided source, use TST_SOURCE_NOT_USED.

codes.name: Arithmetic Slip
codes.plain_name: Calculation slip
codes.student_help: The steps make sense, with a small calculation slip in the numbers.
codes.description: An isolated arithmetic error with a sound method.
codes.example: Population density: 2,000,000 ÷ 50,000 km² = 400 people/km².

tell_apart.how: If the wrong numbers were read from the graph or table, use PRC_DATA_MISREAD; this code is for a slip in the calculation.

codes.remediation: Five-item rapid micro-drill on the same operation.

codes.name: Copy Error
codes.plain_name: Copied a number wrong
codes.student_help: A number or sign changed when copying from one line to the next.
codes.description: Miscopies a digit, sign or term from one of the student's own lines to the next.
codes.example: Copies 1929 from the source as 1992 in the answer.

tell_apart.how: If a value was calculated wrongly rather than copied, use FAC_ARITHMETIC_SLIP.

codes.name: Unclear or Wordy Sentences
codes.plain_name: Sentences are hard to follow
codes.student_help: Say it in fewer words; one idea per sentence is fine.
codes.description: Sentences are so long, wordy or tangled that the meaning is hard to follow, though no single grammar rule is broken.
codes.example: 'The thing about the Depression was that it was a time when the things that happened were very bad for many reasons.'

tell_apart.how: If the problem is the order of ideas, use STR_ILLOGICAL_ORDER.

codes.name: Informal Register
codes.plain_name: Too casual for the task
codes.student_help: In formal writing avoid slang, contractions and 'you'.
codes.description: Uses slang, contractions, text-speak, second person or a chatty tone where a formal register is expected.
codes.example: 'Basically the government was super mean to the strikers.'

tell_apart.how: If a specific subject term is missing, use COM_IMPRECISE_TERMS.

codes.name: Imprecise Terms
codes.plain_name: Used an everyday word where a subject term was needed
codes.student_help: Use the exact subject word instead of an everyday one.
codes.description: The idea is right but is stated with everyday or loose words where a specific scientific term is needed, so the answer is ambiguous.
codes.example: 'The government made people join the army' (conscription); 'more people moved to cities' with no 'urbanisation' when asked to define trends.

tell_apart.how: If the student uses the wrong term, use FAC_NAME_TERM_RECALL.

codes.name: Citation Format
codes.plain_name: Quote or source cited incorrectly
codes.student_help: Cite with the format your teacher uses (for example MLA: (Golding 45)).
codes.description: Missing or wrongly formatted citations, page references or works cited entries; quotations not marked as quotations.
codes.example: Uses a sentence from a website with no quotation marks or source.

tell_apart.how: If the source is cited but not evaluated, use PRC_SOURCE_AT_FACE_VALUE.

codes.name: Map or Graph Conventions Missing
codes.plain_name: Map or graph missing title, legend or scale
codes.student_help: Maps need a title, legend, scale, north arrow and labels; graphs need a title, labelled axes and units.
codes.description: A map or graph the student made is missing required conventions (title, orientation, date, author, legend, scale, labels).
codes.example: Thematic map with colours but no legend or title.

tell_apart.how: PRC_DATA_MISREAD is about reading a map or graph; this code is about making one.

codes.name: Unsupported Answer
codes.plain_name: Answer not explained
codes.student_help: The answer is there, but the reason the question asked for is missing.
codes.description: Gives an answer, claim or 'show that' conclusion without the reasoning or working the question requires.
codes.example: 'Was the Treaty of Versailles fair to Germany? No.'

tell_apart.how: If reasoning is given but no specific evidence, use PRC_NO_EVIDENCE.

codes.name: Blank / Time Attrition
codes.plain_name: Left blank
codes.student_help: This part was left blank.
codes.description: Leaves a question or part with no attempt, from time pressure or a frustration block.
codes.example: Leaves the source-analysis question blank.

tell_apart.how: If any work was started, use TST_ABANDONED_WORK.
If other parts of the same question are answered, use TST_SKIPPED_PART.
If something was written but far too little, use TST_LENGTH_MISMATCH.

codes.remediation: Prerequisite baseline probe on that topic.

codes.name: Skipped Part
codes.plain_name: Part of the question skipped
codes.student_help: One part of the question was skipped while the others were answered.
codes.description: Answers some parts of a multi-part question and leaves another out, likely without noticing.
codes.example: Asked for one cause and one consequence; gives only the cause.

tell_apart.how: If the whole question is empty, use TST_BLANK.

codes.name: Abandoned Work
codes.plain_name: Gave up partway
codes.student_help: A good start was stopped or crossed out before reaching an answer.
codes.description: Starts a valid approach, then stops or crosses it out partway with no answer.
codes.example: Starts the essay outline, writes the thesis, then stops.

tell_apart.how: If nothing was written, use TST_BLANK.

codes.remediation: First-step confidence warm-up, then the same problem.

codes.name: Length Mismatch
codes.plain_name: Much too short or too long
codes.student_help: Check the length asked for (words, paragraphs, lines) and plan to fit it.
codes.description: Writes far less or far more than the task asks for (a paragraph for an essay, one sentence where a series of paragraphs is set).
codes.example: Two sentences for a question worth 10 marks.

tell_apart.how: If the writing stops mid-thought, use TST_ABANDONED_WORK.

codes.name: Provided Source Not Used
codes.plain_name: Didn't use the source you were given
codes.student_help: When a question gives you a source, quote or point to it in your answer.
codes.description: Answers a source-based question from memory or general knowledge without using the provided source, or gets a fact wrong that the source states.
codes.example: Asked what Source B suggests about public opinion, writes about the war in general.

tell_apart.how: If the source is used but not questioned, use PRC_SOURCE_AT_FACE_VALUE.

codes.name: Tempting Wrong Option
codes.plain_name: Picked an answer that sounds right but isn't supported
codes.student_help: Check each option against the passage, not against what sounds true.
codes.description: In a multiple-choice reading question, picks an option that is true in general, uses words from the passage, or is half right, instead of the one the passage supports.
codes.example: Picks 'Canada fought in WWI' when the question asks what the source says about conscription.

tell_apart.how: For written answers that ignore the source, use TST_SOURCE_NOT_USED.
